subModules.title: Reading Mission: Calm Conversations and Helpful Solutions

content.summary: In this mission, you will read about how customer support agents calm upset clients, accept feedback politely, and solve service problems without placing blame on anyone.

linguisticTarget.grammar: Apologies with 'sorry for' / 'apologise that', polite passives (e.g., 'the mistake has been corrected'), and modal verbs for solutions (should, ought to, had better).
linguisticTarget.vocabulary: Key terms for handling customer issues, such as de-escalate, inconvenience, resolve, acknowledge, and compensation.
linguisticTarget.readingStrategy: Scanning for problem-and-solution structures and noticing polite phrases in formal emails and customer service dialogues.

learningObjectives: Understand the main idea of a professional customer service case study.
Locate specific details about client complaints, reasons for delay, and proposed solutions.
Recognize and interpret polite passive voice structures and empathetic apologies in written messages.

contextWarmup.prompt: Imagine an angry customer sends an email because their order arrived three days late. What is the best first step to take?
options: Acknowledge their frustration immediately and say sorry for the delay.
Explain that the delivery driver was lazy and avoid taking responsibility.
Tell the customer to calm down and ignore the email for two days.
contextWarmup.explanation: Acknowledging the problem and apologizing for the inconvenience calms the customer down and establishes a respectful conversation.

rules: Rule 1: Use empathetic phrases like 'I apologise for the inconvenience' or 'I am really sorry that you experienced this delay' to make customers feel heard.
Rule 2: Use the passive voice (e.g., 'The error has been reviewed' or 'A replacement will be dispatched') to focus on the fix instead of pointing fingers at colleagues.
Rule 3: Suggest constructive actions using 'we should' or 'we ought to', and reserve 'had better' for urgent situations that need immediate attention.

commonTrap.trapTitle: Blaming People Instead of Fixing Problems
commonTrap.explanation: Learners often say 'My colleague forgot your order' or 'You did not read the terms'. This makes the client angrier. Always use calm, passive sentences and take collective ownership.
commonTrap.wrong: My colleague made an error and forgot to send your receipt.
commonTrap.correct: An error was made with the receipt, and a new copy has been sent to your email.

content.passageTitle: Turning an Angry Client into a Loyal Friend
paragraphs: At Apex Office Supplies, customer service specialist Maya opened an urgent email on Monday morning. Mr. Henderson, a long-time corporate client, was furious. His office had ordered thirty ergonomic chairs two weeks earlier for a new department opening, but the delivery had arrived with only twelve chairs. Even worse, five of those chairs had scratched armrests. In his message, Mr. Henderson threatened to cancel his annual contract immediately.

Maya knew she needed to act fast to de-escalate the tension. Instead of making excuses or blaming the warehouse staff, she drafted a prompt and polite reply. First, she wrote, 'I sincerely apologise for the stress and inconvenience this delay has caused your team.' Next, she acknowledged the mistake clearly, writing that the order had been packed incorrectly due to an inventory update. By doing this, she validated the customer's frustration.

To fix the problem, Maya outlined clear next steps without making Mr. Henderson do extra work. She explained that the remaining eighteen chairs had already been loaded onto an express van and would arrive by 2:00 PM that afternoon. Furthermore, replacements for the five damaged chairs had been arranged free of charge. She added, 'We ought to make sure your department opening runs smoothly today, so our technician will assemble them on site.'

Finally, Maya discussed compensation. As a gesture of goodwill, a thirty percent discount was applied to the entire invoice, and a credit voucher was added to Mr. Henderson's account for future orders. Mr. Henderson replied two hours later, thanking Maya for her quick, honest action. By handling the complaint with empathy and clear solutions, Maya saved a valuable business relationship.

subModules.title: Writing Mission: Calm and Helpful Customer Care

content.summary: Write clear, polite replies to customer complaints. First, show that you understand the problem and apologise. Next, explain what action has been taken without blaming a person. Finally, offer a practical solution and say what will happen next.

blueprintItems.title: Step 1: Show Empathy and Apologise
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + apologise / am sorry + that-clause or for + noun / gerund
blueprintItems.example: I'm really sorry for the inconvenience you've experienced with your order.

blueprintItems.title: Step 2: Explain the Action Politely
blueprintItems.formula: Subject + has / have been + past participle
blueprintItems.example: Your complaint has been forwarded to our senior team.

blueprintItems.title: Step 3: Offer a Practical Solution
blueprintItems.formula: We should / ought to / had better + base verb
blueprintItems.example: We should arrange a full refund or send you a replacement.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a comma after a short opening such as 'Dear Ms Green' only if your chosen greeting style requires it. Start the message body with a capital letter.
mechanicsRules.badExample: dear ms green, we are sorry for the delay.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Dear Ms Green, We are sorry for the delay.
mechanicsRules.why: Capitalize the first word of a sentence and people's names.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use a full stop at the end of a complete sentence. Use a question mark only for a direct question.
mechanicsRules.badExample: Your refund has been arranged, Can you confirm your address.
mechanicsRules.goodExample: Your refund has been arranged. Can you confirm your address?
mechanicsRules.why: A full stop separates statements, and a question mark ends a direct question.

mechanicsRules.rule: Use 'has been' with a singular subject and 'have been' with a plural subject or 'you'.
mechanicsRules.why: The helping verb must agree with the subject.

subModules.title: Speaking Lab: Calm, Clear Customer Service

content.summary: Practise responding to complaints with a calm voice, clear explanations, and practical solutions. Acknowledge the problem, show empathy, explain what can be done, and check that the customer understands.
content.audioGuidance: Speak at a steady pace and use a warm, respectful tone. Stress important words such as apologise, resolve, and compensation. Let your voice fall at the end of clear statements. Use a gentle rising tone when checking or asking a question.

pillars.name: Vowel Clarity
pillars.target: Clear vowel sounds in customer service vocabulary
pillars.explanation: Say each vowel clearly in words such as issue, refund, and inconvenience. Avoid rushing long words, and pronounce their syllables in order.

pillars.name: Word Stress
pillars.target: Stress the correct syllable in longer words
pillars.explanation: Give the strongest beat to the stressed syllable in words such as compensation and inconvenience. This helps customers understand you.

pillars.name: Calm Intonation
pillars.explanation: Keep your voice calm when a customer is upset. Use a soft rising tone for polite checks and a falling tone for clear offers or promises.

pillars.name: Clear Phrasing
pillars.target: Pause between the problem and the solution
pillars.explanation: Use short phrases and small pauses. For example, acknowledge the problem first, then explain what you will do next.

stressPairs.shiftExplanation: In inconvenience, stress the second syllable. In compensation, stress the third syllable.
Acknowledge has stress on the second syllable. Resolve also has stress on its second syllable.
Escalate has stress on the final syllable, while apologise has stress on the first.
Refund is stressed on the second syllable. Apology is stressed on the second syllable too.

reading.question: What was the main reason for Mr. Henderson's angry email?
options: His order arrived incomplete and several items were damaged.
He wanted to cancel his contract because prices were too high.
The delivery team arrived three weeks earlier than expected.
reading.answer: His order arrived incomplete and several items were damaged.
reading.explanation: Paragraph 1 mentions that out of thirty chairs ordered, only twelve arrived, and five had scratched armrests.

reading.question: How many chairs were missing from the initial delivery?
options: Twelve chairs
Eighteen chairs
Five chairs
reading.explanation: Mr. Henderson ordered thirty chairs and received twelve, which means eighteen chairs were still missing.

reading.question: What did Maya avoid doing when answering Mr. Henderson's email?
options: She avoided offering any discounts or vouchers.
She avoided blaming warehouse staff or making excuses.
She avoided replying until the next working day.
reading.answer: She avoided blaming warehouse staff or making excuses.
reading.explanation: Paragraph 2 states that 'Instead of making excuses or blaming the warehouse staff, she drafted a prompt and polite reply.'

reading.question: Why did Maya state that the order was packed incorrectly?
options: Because of a system crash during checkout.
Because an inventory update caused a mistake.
Because the warehouse was closed for maintenance.
reading.answer: Because an inventory update caused a mistake.
reading.explanation: In paragraph 2, Maya explained that the order had been packed incorrectly due to an inventory update.

reading.question: When were the remaining eighteen chairs scheduled to arrive?
options: By 2:00 PM that afternoon
The following Monday morning
Within five business days
reading.explanation: Paragraph 3 notes that the chairs had been loaded onto an express van and would arrive by 2:00 PM that afternoon.

reading.question: What extra service did Maya offer regarding the damaged chairs?
options: A technician would assemble the replacement chairs on site.
Mr. Henderson would have to repair the armrests himself.
The client had to ship the damaged chairs back before getting replacements.
reading.answer: A technician would assemble the replacement chairs on site.
reading.explanation: Maya said their technician would assemble the chairs on site to ensure the opening ran smoothly.

reading.question: Which forms of compensation did Apex Office Supplies offer to Mr. Henderson?
options: A thirty percent discount on the invoice and a credit voucher for future orders
A complete refund of the entire contract and free desks
A ten percent discount on the next purchase only
reading.answer: A thirty percent discount on the invoice and a credit voucher for future orders
reading.explanation: Paragraph 4 explains that a thirty percent discount was applied to the entire invoice along with a credit voucher.

reading.question: What does the word 'de-escalate' mean in paragraph 2?
options: To increase the cost of shipping
To calm an intense or angry situation
To cancel a contract immediately
reading.answer: To calm an intense or angry situation
reading.explanation: To de-escalate means to reduce tension and make a difficult situation calmer.

reading.question: How did Mr. Henderson respond after receiving Maya's solution?
options: He refused the offer and called a lawyer.
He thanked Maya for her quick and honest action.
He asked for a different support agent.
reading.answer: He thanked Maya for her quick and honest action.
reading.explanation: Paragraph 4 states that Mr. Henderson replied two hours later, thanking Maya for her quick, honest action.

reading.question: What is the key lesson about handling complaints from this text?
options: Companies should wait several days before replying so clients calm down.
Using empathy and providing prompt solutions helps protect client relationships.
Support staff should always transfer every complaint to a senior manager.
reading.answer: Using empathy and providing prompt solutions helps protect client relationships.
reading.explanation: The final sentence highlights that handling complaints with empathy and clear solutions saved a valuable relationship.

reading.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses must be enclosed by commas on both sides.

reading.question: What does the expression 'think outside the box' convey in an entrepreneurial context?
options: Approach problems with non-traditional and creative perspectives.
Store physical inventory outside the warehouse boundaries.
Follow standard operating procedures without deviation.
Ignore financial accounting standards during quarterly audits.
reading.answer: Approach problems with non-traditional and creative perspectives.
reading.explanation: The idiom 'think outside the box' signifies lateral and innovative thinking.

reading.question: Choose the correct reported speech: '"I have submitted the report," said David.'
options: David said that he had submitted the report.

reading.answer: David said that he had submitted the report.
reading.explanation: Present perfect in direct speech backshifts to past perfect in reported speech.

options: 'Economic' relates to the economy, whereas 'economical' means avoiding waste or saving money.
'Economic' means inexpensive, whereas 'economical' relates to government finance.

'Economical' is only used as a noun, whereas 'economic' is an adverb.

writing.instruction: Rewrite the sentence to apologise using 'sorry for'.
writing.promptText: The customer had to wait for a long time.
writing.hint: Use 'I'm sorry for' followed by a noun or gerund phrase.
targetAnswers: I'm sorry for the long wait.
I'm sorry for making you wait for a long time.
writing.explanation: Use 'sorry for' before a noun or a verb ending in '-ing' to apologise for an experience or action.

writing.instruction: Change the sentence to a polite passive form.
writing.promptText: Our team has forwarded your complaint to the manager.
writing.hint: Make 'your complaint' the subject and use 'has been' plus a past participle.
targetAnswers: Your complaint has been forwarded to the manager.
Your complaint has been forwarded to the manager by our team.
writing.explanation: The passive form puts the focus on the complaint and the action, rather than on the person who did it.

writing.instruction: Complete the offer with 'should' and the base verb.
targetAnswers: We should send a replacement to you.
writing.explanation: Use 'should' followed by the base verb to make a polite suggestion.

writing.instruction: Join the ideas with 'but' to show a problem and a helpful action.
writing.promptText: Your refund has been approved. It may take three days to reach your account.
writing.hint: Use a comma before 'but' when it joins two complete sentences.
targetAnswers: Your refund has been approved, but it may take three days to reach your account.
writing.explanation: 'But' links two contrasting ideas. Use a comma before it when both parts can stand as complete sentences.

writing.instruction: Join the ideas with 'because' to give the reason for the action.
writing.promptText: We have sent a replacement. Your item was damaged.
targetAnswers: We have sent a replacement because your item was damaged.
writing.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for an action.

writing.instruction: Complete the sentence with 'and' to add the next action.
writing.promptText: Your report has been received, ______ we will contact you tomorrow.
writing.hint: Use the conjunction that adds information.
targetAnswers: Your report has been received, and we will contact you tomorrow.
writing.explanation: Use 'and' to connect two related ideas. Put a comma before it when it joins two complete sentences.

writing.instruction: Correct the capital letters, verb form, and punctuation.
writing.hint: Start with a capital letter, use 'has been' with 'payment', and add a full stop.
targetAnswers: Your payment has been checked.
writing.explanation: 'Payment' is singular, so use 'has been'. Begin the sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.

writing.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capital letters.

writing.hint: Capitalize the greeting and the first word of the message. Use punctuation to separate them.
targetAnswers: Dear Mr Brown, we are sorry for the delay.
Dear Mr Brown, We are sorry for the delay.
writing.explanation: Capitalize titles and names. Separate the greeting from the message with a comma, and end the statement with a full stop.

writing.instruction: Write one polite sentence to apologise to a customer whose order arrived late.

practicumQuestions.promptText: The customer had to wait for a long time.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I'm sorry for' followed by a noun or gerund phrase.
targetAnswers: I'm sorry for the long wait.
I'm sorry for making you wait for a long time.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'sorry for' before a noun or a verb ending in '-ing' to apologise for an experience or action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the sentence to a polite passive form.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Our team has forwarded your complaint to the manager.
practicumQuestions.hint: Make 'your complaint' the subject and use 'has been' plus a past participle.
targetAnswers: Your complaint has been forwarded to the manager.
Your complaint has been forwarded to the manager by our team.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passive form puts the focus on the complaint and the action, rather than on the person who did it.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the offer with 'should' and the base verb.
practicumQuestions.promptText: We ______ a replacement to you.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'send' after 'should'.
targetAnswers: We should send a replacement to you.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'should' followed by the base verb to make a polite suggestion.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas with 'but' to show a problem and a helpful action.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Your refund has been approved. It may take three days to reach your account.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use a comma before 'but' when it joins two complete sentences.
targetAnswers: Your refund has been approved, but it may take three days to reach your account.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'But' links two contrasting ideas. Use a comma before it when both parts can stand as complete sentences.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Join the ideas with 'because' to give the reason for the action.
practicumQuestions.promptText: We have sent a replacement. Your item was damaged.
practicumQuestions.hint: Put the reason after 'because'.
targetAnswers: We have sent a replacement because your item was damaged.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Because' introduces the reason for an action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Complete the sentence with 'and' to add the next action.
practicumQuestions.promptText: Your report has been received, ______ we will contact you tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.hint: Use the conjunction that adds information.
targetAnswers: Your report has been received, and we will contact you tomorrow.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use 'and' to connect two related ideas. Put a comma before it when it joins two complete sentences.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the capital letters, verb form, and punctuation.
practicumQuestions.promptText: your payment have been checked
practicumQuestions.hint: Start with a capital letter, use 'has been' with 'payment', and add a full stop.
targetAnswers: Your payment has been checked.
practicumQuestions.explanation: 'Payment' is singular, so use 'has been'. Begin the sentence with a capital letter and end it with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Correct the punctuation and capital letters.
practicumQuestions.promptText: dear mr brown we are sorry for the delay
practicumQuestions.hint: Capitalize the greeting and the first word of the message. Use punctuation to separate them.
targetAnswers: Dear Mr Brown, we are sorry for the delay.
Dear Mr Brown, We are sorry for the delay.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Capitalize titles and names. Separate the greeting from the message with a comma, and end the statement with a full stop.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write one polite sentence to apologise to a customer whose order arrived late.
practicumQuestions.promptText: The customer says: 'My order arrived three days late.'
practicumQuestions.hint: Use 'I'm sorry that' or 'I'm sorry for'.
targetAnswers: I'm sorry that your order arrived late.
I'm sorry for the delay with your order.
practicumQuestions.explanation: A direct apology recognises the customer's problem and uses a polite, clear tone.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Write two short sentences. Use a passive form to describe an action, then offer a solution with 'should'.
practicumQuestions.promptText: A customer received the wrong item.
practicumQuestions.hint: You could say that the order has been checked, then offer to send the correct item.
targetAnswers: Your order has been checked. We should send the correct item today.
The mistake has been reported to our team. We should arrange a replacement for you.
practicumQuestions.explanation: The passive form keeps attention on the action, and 'should' introduces a practical suggestion.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about a time when a service did not meet your expectations.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Tell me about a problem you had with a product or service and how you dealt with it.
storyPoints: What you bought or what service you used
What went wrong and how it affected you
How you contacted the company and what solution you received
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: My delivery arrived late, so I contacted customer service and asked them to resolve the problem.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /maɪ dɪˈlɪvəri əˈraɪvd leɪt səʊ aɪ ˈkɒntæktɪd ˈkʌstəmə ˈsɜːvɪs/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Tell the events in a clear order. Use past tense for what happened and explain how you felt.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Speak for at least 20 seconds about how you would help an unhappy customer.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Imagine a customer is angry because they were charged twice. Explain what you would say and do.
storyPoints: How you would acknowledge the billing error
How you would apologise and show empathy
What action you would take to resolve the issue
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I would acknowledge the error, apologise for the inconvenience, and make sure the extra charge was refunded.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /aɪ wʊd əkˈnɒlɪdʒ ði ˈerə əˈpɒlədʒaɪz fə ði ˌɪnkənˈviːniəns/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use polite language and explain each step in a calm, helpful way.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the service agent. Calm the customer, acknowledge the complaint, and offer a practical solution.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: The customer says their online order has not arrived and they are angry.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer has waited five days beyond the expected delivery date. They call to complain and want to know what will happen next.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a customer service agent. Apologise for the delay, check the order, and explain that you will arrange a replacement or delivery update.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Acknowledge the problem before you explain what action you can take.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the service agent. Recognise the billing problem and explain how it will be corrected.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: The customer says they were charged twice and wants their money back.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer can see two charges for one purchase on their bank statement. They are worried that the extra money will not be returned.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a service agent. Acknowledge the error, apologise, and explain politely that the extra charge will be refunded after you check the account.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use a calm voice and a polite passive sentence such as, “The extra charge will be refunded.”

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the service agent. Show empathy and suggest fair compensation for the service problem.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: The customer says a repair appointment was cancelled twice and asks for compensation.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer has taken time off work for two repair appointments, but both were cancelled. They are frustrated and ask the company to make up for the inconvenience.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a service agent. Apologise for the inconvenience, offer available compensation, and arrange a new appointment.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Recognise the time the customer has lost and offer a clear next step.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Respond as the service agent. Offer to pass the complaint to a more senior person if needed.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: The customer says they have contacted the company before and are not satisfied with the response.
practicumQuestions.scenarioContext: A customer has contacted the company twice about a faulty product. They are unhappy with the previous replies and want someone else to review the case.
practicumQuestions.characterRole: You are a service agent. Listen carefully, acknowledge the customer’s concern, and offer to escalate the complaint to a senior manager.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Do not argue. Confirm that you understand the concern and explain how the complaint can be escalated.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use the words de-escalate, acknowledge, resolve, and compensation in short customer service sentences.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: A customer is upset about a delayed order. Tell them how you will recognise the problem and help.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: I acknowledge the delay, and I will resolve the issue by arranging a replacement with compensation.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use each word in a sentence that fits its meaning. Speak calmly and make your offer clear.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Change the direct sentences into polite passive sentences about customer service actions.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say a polite passive sentence about a refund, a complaint review, or a problem being fixed.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Your complaint will be reviewed, and the issue will be resolved as soon as possible.
practicumQuestions.explanation: Use will be followed by a past participle to describe a polite service action.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Say each word clearly and put the main stress on the correct syllable.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Repeat inconvenience, compensation, acknowledge, and resolve. Make the stressed syllable stronger.
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: We apologise for the inconvenience and will resolve the problem.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wi əˈpɒlədʒaɪz fə ði ˌɪnkənˈviːniəns ənd wɪl rɪˈzɒlv ðə ˈprɒbləm/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Stress the second syllable in inconvenience and resolve, and the third syllable in compensation.

practicumQuestions.instruction: Use a gentle rising tone for the polite question and a falling tone for the clear offer.
practicumQuestions.audioPrompt: Say, “Would you like me to escalate your complaint?” Then say, “I can arrange a refund for you.”
practicumQuestions.targetSentence: Would you like me to escalate your complaint? I can arrange a refund for you.
practicumQuestions.phonetic: /wʊd ju laɪk mi tə ˈeskəleɪt jɔː kəmˈpleɪnt | aɪ kən əˈreɪndʒ ə ˈriːfʌnd fə juː/
practicumQuestions.explanation: Let your voice rise gently at the end of the polite question. Let it fall at the end of the offer.
